hook: This is a full locked-room murder mystery told entirely through Foundation paperwork: an inventory, interview transcripts, a test video, and a closing presentation where the investigator gathers every suspect in one room. The victim is a crime novelist whose books came true when she reread them, so keep that rule in mind from the first page. Expect a brutal stabbing, foul language and one interview with a serial sex offender, and read slowly: the clues really are on the page.
whyItMatters: Most SCP articles use interviews as texture, but this one turns the format into a classic whodunit, complete with alibis, red herrings and a parlour-room reveal. It carries the meta tag for good reason: the anomaly is about authorship, and the story keeps asking who is writing whom. It is a good example of how the wiki can host a straight genre piece without losing the Foundation's clinical voice.
thingsToNotice: Almost everyone in Wing G is lying about something other than the murder, and O'Connor solves it by lining the lies up. Grossenbacher is blackmailing the Site Director over doctored reality-anchor reports; Director May is really Eve Holloway, mother of the student killed in the newspaper clipping, who placed a wall-walking serial rapist in the wing and switched off his anchor so he would torment Emma; Simpson has joined the Serpent's Hand and came in with a stolen knife to help her escape; and Dr. Yau was secretly sleeping with Emma and had edited the cameras to hide it. Emma refused to leave because of Yau, Simpson fled leaving the knife and the door unlocked, and the casually mentioned habit of rattling cell doors in both directions is what exposes the real killer. Officer Lowry, drunk and back from his smoke break, found the door open, heard Emma flaunt the affair with the woman he was infatuated with, and stabbed her, then staged the discovery; the stray whisky bottle is his one mistake. The afterword reopens everything: the scissor-cut blank pages may be a grille cipher that turns her novel into a second text, which would make her death a suicide written through Lowry. O'Connor then asks whether her own report reads like a summary or like a story, notes she was born before Emma ever wrote, and hopes that you, the reader, are real too.
